Fubini–Tonelli Theorem

Iterated integrals agree in either order. Sum the rows first or the columns first, the total is the same.

For nonnegative functions this is always safe. For integrable functions it is safe too. Without integrability, the two orders can split apart.

For example, count 🍎 apples packed in a grid inside a 📦 box: counting by rows or by columns gives the same total.

∬f=∫ ⁣ ⁣(∫f dx) ⁣dy=∫ ⁣ ⁣(∫f dy) ⁣dx\iint f = \int\!\!\left(\int f\,dx\right)\!dy = \int\!\!\left(\int f\,dy\right)\!dx∬f=∫(∫fdx)dy=∫(∫fdy)dx

For f(x,y)=xyf(x, y) = xyf(x,y)=xy (on [0,1]2[0,1]^2[0,1]2), compute both iterated integrals ∫01 ⁣ ⁣∫01xy dx dy\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 xy\,dx\,dy∫01​∫01​xydxdy and ∫01 ⁣ ⁣∫01xy dy dx\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 xy\,dy\,dx∫01​∫01​xydydx directly and show each equals 14\frac1441​.

∫01 ⁣ ⁣∫01xy dx dy=∫01y2 dy=14=∫01 ⁣ ⁣∫01xy dy dx\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 xy\,dx\,dy = \int_0^1 \frac{y}{2}\,dy = \frac{1}{4} = \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 xy\,dy\,dx∫01​∫01​xydxdy=∫01​2y​dy=41​=∫01​∫01​xydydx

  2. Reversing the order: for fixed xxx, ∫01xy dy=x⋅12\int_0^1 xy\,dy = x \cdot \frac12∫01​xydy=x⋅21​, and ∫01x2 dx=14\int_0^1 \frac{x}{2}\,dx = \frac14∫01​2x​dx=41​. Both orders give 14\frac1441​ — because the product splits: ∬xy=(∫01x dx)(∫01y dy)\iint xy = (\int_0^1 x\,dx)(\int_0^1 y\,dy)∬xy=(∫01​xdx)(∫01​ydy).

The function f(x,y)=xyf(x,y) = xyf(x,y)=xy is continuous on [0,1]2[0,1]^2[0,1]2, hence measurable, and f≥0f \ge 0f≥0, so all hypotheses of Tonelli's theorem are satisfied and Tonelli's theorem guarantees the value is order-independent — the direct computation above verifies the theorem on this concrete function. Every step is complete.

Before invoking the contrapositive, verify measurability and almost-everywhere inner integrability: fff is continuous on (0,1]2(0,1]^2(0,1]2, hence measurable on [0,1]2[0,1]^2[0,1]2 (define fff arbitrarily at the single point (0,0)(0,0)(0,0); a single point and the coordinate segments {x=0}\{x=0\}{x=0}, {y=0}\{y=0\}{y=0} have measure zero).

    As shown above, the inner integrals exist for every x>0x > 0x>0 (resp. y>0y > 0y>0), i.e. for almost every xxx (resp. yyy). Since ∣f∣|f|∣f∣ is measurable and ≥0\ge 0≥0, Tonelli applied to ∣f∣|f|∣f∣ legitimately gives ∫∣f∣=∞\int |f| = \infty∫∣f∣=∞.

    Hence, by contrapositive, fff is not integrable over (0,1)2(0,1)^2(0,1)2 (∫∣f∣=∞\int |f| = \infty∫∣f∣=∞) — without the integrability hypothesis, signed mass cancels differently depending on the order.

    The sign-flip symmetry was proved with no computation, and the π/4\pi/4π/4 evaluation is fully justified via antiderivatives and improper integrals. Every step is complete.

For a simple function f≥0f \ge 0f≥0, prove both iterated integrals equal the double sum ∑ak m(Ek)\sum a_k\,m(E_k)∑ak​m(Ek​) (with no integrability hypothesis), and extend to general f≥0f \ge 0f≥0 by monotone approximation.

For a simple function built from rectangles, s=∑p=1Pcp 1Ap×Bps = \sum_{p=1}^{P} c_p\,\mathbf{1}_{A_p \times B_p}s=∑p=1P​cp​1Ap​×Bp​​ (cp≥0c_p \ge 0cp​≥0, disjoint rectangles), sections are explicit and no lemma is needed: for fixed yyy, ∫s(x,y) dx=∑pcp m(Ap) 1Bp(y)\int s(x,y)\,dx = \sum_p c_p\,m(A_p)\,\mathbf{1}_{B_p}(y)∫s(x,y)dx=∑p​cp​m(Ap​)1Bp​​(y) (previous step), a simple function of yyy, so the outer integral is ∑pcp m(Ap) m(Bp)\sum_p c_p\,m(A_p)\,m(B_p)∑p​cp​m(Ap​)m(Bp​) — the same with the order reversed.

    ∫ ⁣ ⁣∫∑pcp 1Ap×Bp=∑pcp m(Ap) m(Bp)(either order)\int\!\!\int \sum_p c_p\,\mathbf{1}_{A_p \times B_p} = \sum_p c_p\,m(A_p)\,m(B_p) \quad \text{(either order)}∫∫p∑​cp​1Ap​×Bp​​=p∑​cp​m(Ap​)m(Bp​)(either order)

Lemma (measurable sections): on a finite-measure product space (e.g. [0,1]2[0,1]^2[0,1]2), if EEE is product-measurable then each section Ey={x:(x,y)∈E}E^y = \{x : (x,y) \in E\}Ey={x:(x,y)∈E} is measurable, y↦m(Ey)y \mapsto m(E^y)y↦m(Ey) is measurable, and ∫m(Ey) dy=m(E)\int m(E^y)\,dy = m(E)∫m(Ey)dy=m(E) (same for xxx-sections). Proof: first let A\mathcal{A}A be the collection of finite disjoint unions of measurable rectangles; A\mathcal{A}A is an algebra (closed under complements and finite unions) and generates the product σ\sigmaσ-algebra, σ(A)\sigma(\mathcal{A})σ(A) being the product σ\sigmaσ-algebra.

    The family C\mathcal{C}C of sets with this property contains every rectangle — for E=A×BE = A \times BE=A×B, Ey=AE^y = AEy=A (y∈By \in By∈B) or ∅\varnothing∅, and m(Ey)=m(A) 1B(y)m(E^y) = m(A)\,\mathbf{1}_B(y)m(Ey)=m(A)1B​(y) — and by finite additivity the section-measure identity holds on all of A\mathcal{A}A, so A⊂C\mathcal{A} \subset \mathcal{C}A⊂C. Moreover C\mathcal{C}C is a monotone class: if En↑EE_n \uparrow EEn​↑E then (En)y↑Ey(E_n)^y \uparrow E^y(En​)y↑Ey, so continuity of measure plus MCT gives ∫m((En)y) dy=m(En)↑m(E)=∫m(Ey) dy\int m((E_n)^y)\,dy = m(E_n) \uparrow m(E) = \int m(E^y)\,dy∫m((En​)y)dy=m(En​)↑m(E)=∫m(Ey)dy (decreasing sequences likewise, using finite measure).

    By the monotone class theorem, C\mathcal{C}C contains σ(A)\sigma(\mathcal{A})σ(A), so C\mathcal{C}C is the whole product σ\sigmaσ-algebra.

For a general simple function f=∑k=1mak 1Ekf = \sum_{k=1}^{m} a_k\,\mathbf{1}_{E_k}f=∑k=1m​ak​1Ek​​ (ak≥0a_k \ge 0ak​≥0, the EkE_kEk​ disjoint product-measurable): the section fy(x)=f(x,y)=∑kak 1(Ek)y(x)f^y(x) = f(x,y) = \sum_k a_k\,\mathbf{1}_{(E_k)^y}(x)fy(x)=f(x,y)=∑k​ak​1(Ek​)y​(x) is simple, so ∫fy dx=∑kak m((Ek)y)\int f^y\,dx = \sum_k a_k\,m((E_k)^y)∫fydx=∑k​ak​m((Ek​)y) — and by the lemma, y↦∫fy dxy \mapsto \int f^y\,dxy↦∫fydx is a sum of measurable functions, hence measurable.

    Integrating gives ∫ ⁣ ⁣∫f dx dy=∑kak∫m((Ek)y) dy=∑k=1mak m(Ek)\int\!\!\int f\,dx\,dy = \sum_k a_k \int m((E_k)^y)\,dy = \sum_{k=1}^{m} a_k\,m(E_k)∫∫fdxdy=∑k​ak​∫m((Ek​)y)dy=∑k=1m​ak​m(Ek​) — a single double sum, independent of order.

    Every term is ≥0\ge 0≥0, so nothing can cancel: no integrability hypothesis is needed.

This is why Tonelli's theorem needs no integrability hypothesis for f≥0f \ge 0f≥0 — every step is complete.
